intro: When you search for a conservation architect near me, you are likely looking for someone who understands historic buildings and can guide you through repairs or sensitive alterations. Conservation architects specialise in this work, often with AABC accreditation, and can help you navigate the specific challenges of older properties. We introduce you to a suitable UK professional who will quote you directly, with fees on application.
need_heading: What people searching for a conservation architect usually need
need_lead: You have a historic building and want expert help to repair, alter or maintain it without harming its character.
needs: You own a listed building and need advice on what repairs are allowed and how to approach them.
You are planning an extension or alteration to a period property and want to ensure the work is sensitive to its original fabric.
You have been told by the council that a heritage statement or conservation area consent is required and need professional help.
You want to find a local architect who has experience with traditional materials and techniques, such as lime mortar or stone.
You are considering buying a historic building and want a professional opinion on its condition and potential.
context: "Architect" is a protected title in the UK, so anyone calling themselves an architect must be on the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register and follow its code of conduct. Many practices are also RIBA Chartered Practices. Conservation architects often hold additional accreditation from the AABC (Architects Accredited in Building Conservation), which shows they have specialist knowledge in historic buildings.

Before you appoint anyone, check the ARB register and ask for a written appointment that sets out services, fees and responsibilities. Building regulations approval, planning permission and party wall matters are separate processes that your architect can help you navigate.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when enquiring
tell: Describe the type of historic building you have, such as a listed cottage, a Georgian townhouse or a medieval church.
Explain what you want to do — for example, repair a roof, replace windows, or add a modern extension.
Mention whether the building is listed or in a conservation area, and if you already have any planning or listed building consent.
Say whether you need a full architectural service from design to completion, or just advice on a specific issue.
Include your location so we can introduce you to a professional who works in your area.
Let us know if you have a deadline or any particular constraints, such as a budget or grant application.
questions: Are you on the Architects Registration Board register, and do you hold any conservation accreditation such as AABC?
Have you worked on buildings of a similar age and type to mine?
What is your approach to using traditional materials and techniques in repairs?
Will you handle planning applications and listed building consent on my behalf?
How do you structure your fees, and what is included in your written appointment?
Can you provide references from previous conservation projects?

faqs.q: Do I need a conservation architect for a listed building?
faqs.a: Not always legally required, but a conservation architect has specialist knowledge of historic fabric and can help you avoid damaging the building or falling foul of consent rules. They can also guide you through planning and listed building consent processes.
AABC stands for Architects Accredited in Building Conservation. It is a recognised accreditation that shows an architect has demonstrated experience and competence in building conservation.

faqs.q: Are grants available for historic building repairs?
faqs.a: Grants may be available from organisations such as Historic England or local authorities, but eligibility and availability vary. A conservation architect can advise on potential funding sources for your project.

faqs.q: How do I check if someone is a registered architect?
faqs.a: You can check the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register online. Only those on the register can call themselves architects, and they must follow the ARB code of conduct and hold professional indemnity insurance.

extra_heading: Choosing a conservation architect near you
extra: Searching for a conservation architect near me suggests you want someone who can visit your historic building easily and who knows the local planning authority and its approach to heritage. Being nearby also helps with site visits during repairs and makes it simpler to discuss details in person. When you compare professionals, ask how familiar they are with your type of building and the local conservation area or listed building context.

Accreditation is a useful starting point: look for AABC (Architects Accredited in Building Conservation) or RIBA conservation accreditation, which show a specialist interest and experience in historic work. But accreditation alone does not tell you whether someone is right for your project, so ask about their approach to traditional materials and how they have handled similar repairs or alterations. Also check that anyone calling themselves an architect is on the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register, as the title is protected in the UK.

At a first appointment, expect to talk through the building's history, its condition and what you hope to achieve. A conservation architect will want to understand any existing consents and may suggest a survey or further investigation before advising on repairs or alterations. Use the meeting to ask how they would approach your project, what their fees cover and how they would keep you informed as the work progresses.

extra_faqs.q: How do I compare conservation architects near me?
extra_faqs.a: Start by checking their accreditation and ARB registration, then ask about their experience with buildings like yours. It also helps to discuss their approach to repairs and materials, and to compare written appointments that set out services and fees.

extra_faqs.q: What should I have ready for a first meeting with a conservation architect?
extra_faqs.a: Gather any information you have about the building, such as its age, listing status and any previous surveys or consents. It is also useful to have a clear idea of what you want to achieve and any constraints, such as budget or timescales.
